title: Timing Matters Twice: When to Query and When to Skip in Flow-Matching On-Policy Distillation.

paper.title: Timing Matters Twice: When to Query and When to Skip in Flow-Matching On-Policy Distillation.
paper.abstract:
Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) enables flow-matching models to acquire complementary capabilities from specialized teachers through supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, different evaluation dimensions (e.g., aesthetics and OCR accuracy) and tasks (e.g., image generation and editing) emphasize different aspects of the denoising process, suggesting that their effective supervision may occur at different stages. Existing methods typically select supervision states from predefined timestep distributions, which may overlook these phase-dependent differences with unnecessary computation overhead. This motivates two critical timing decisions: when to adaptively query teachers for effective supervision based on the evolving generative process, and when to skip the remaining rollout to avoid redundant computation, i.e. , timing matters twice .
In this paper, we introduce PhaseOPD , a phase-aware query-and-skip framework that identifies generative phases online from revisions of predicted-clean latents, using existing student velocity predictions without additional model evaluations. For each task-assigned teacher, PhaseOPD selects a supervision state based on its phase preference and skips the unused rollout suffix once all query decisions are finalized, preserving the single-query velocity-distillation objective.
On SD3.5-M, PhaseOPD executes only 5.56 of 16 rollout positions per local batch (65.2% fewer), reducing training time by 41.3% relative to DanceOPD while improving Aesthetic, GenEval, and OCR scores.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1 : Teacher supervision is not equally useful throughout denoising: semantic composition, text rendering, and aesthetics benefit most from different query intervals. This motivates adapting query timing to each teacher-task pair and terminating the rollout after the required queries, rather than using a shared preset schedule and completing every denoising step. In recent years, diffusion and flow-matching models have made significant progress in image generation [ 7 , 9 , 12 , 16 , 18 ] . The research focus has gradually shifted from improving basic generative capabilities to aligning models with challenging task-specific objectives and preferences through post-training. In complex applications, generative models must satisfy multiple criteria simultaneously, including accurate semantic composition, coherent spatial structure, high-quality local details, and visual appearance aligned with human preferences. Improving multiple visual objectives within a unified model has therefore become an important challenge in generative model post-training. Previous studies have mainly combined reward signals from different evaluation dimensions using weighted aggregation and optimized the generation distribution of pretrained models through reinforcement learning [ 19 , 17 ] . However, such methods not only rely on sparse scalar rewards for optimization, but also suffer from competing update directions induced by heterogeneous rewards, often resulting in gradient interference and imbalanced capabilities. To mitigate reward sparsity and gradient conflicts in joint multi-objective optimization, recent studies have introduced On-Policy Distillation (OPD) into generative models [ 5 , 8 , 20 ] . Instead of directly optimizing a single policy with multiple rewards, multi-teacher OPD first trains specialized teachers independently for different objectives. These teachers then provide supervision on the student’s own generation trajectories, integrating diverse generative capabilities into a unified student model. Although OPD provides an effective approach to multi-objective optimization, existing OPD paradigms do not adequately characterize how the value of each task-specific teacher’s supervision changes across generation stages. Because each teacher is trained for a distinct objective, the key question is which part of the student’s trajectory provides the most effective supervision for that teacher and its corresponding task—not which teacher should be assigned to a given stage. This raises two connected questions: for each teacher-task pair, at what stage should the student be queried to obtain the most useful supervision? Once the relevant query for each task has been completed, when can the remaining rollout be terminated to avoid redundant computation? When query timing is not specified for each teacher-task pair, it remains unclear whether a chosen supervision stage is well suited to that teacher’s objective. This matters because denoising follows a stage-dependent pattern: early stages focus on constructing global semantics, intermediate stages gradually shift toward local content generation, and later stages place greater emphasis on refining details and visual aesthetics. These evolving responsibilities mean that the utility of a given teacher’s guidance depends on whether the student’s state at a particular stage is suitable for that teacher’s corresponding objective. Thus, supervision timing should be determined for each teacher-task pair, rather than by assigning teachers to stages in isolation. Beyond effectively scheduling teacher supervision, avoiding unnecessary computational overhead is another important challenge for multi-teacher OPD. Obtaining teacher supervision requires long and continuous rollouts of student trajectories, which introduces considerable computational costs. More importantly, once all necessary teacher queries have been completed, or once the denoising process is close to convergence and the latent representation has become nearly stationary, continuing the remaining rollout provides little additional information for distillation. It may even introduce optimization conflicts due to a mismatch between teacher supervision and generation dynamics. Therefore, skipping redundant trajectory supervision while preserving its effectiveness is crucial to improving OPD training efficiency. Appendix. A discusses related work in detail. Building on these insights, we propose PhaseOPD, a dual timing-adaptive policy distillation framework that uses the student’s generation dynamics to schedule each task-specific teacher at the stages where its supervision is most useful. Unlike existing methods that focus primarily on task-level teacher selection without jointly optimizing teacher-query timing and trajectory length, PhaseOPD identifies a suitable query interval for each teacher-task pair from the student’s evolving trajectory. For example, it schedules structure-oriented supervision during global layout and primary structure formation, supervision for objectives involving both structure and detail during the transition toward semantic content and salient details, and visual-quality supervision during later texture and appearance refinement. The task-specific teacher defines what is supervised, while the trajectory dynamics determine when its supervision is applied. This constitutes the first level of adaptivity in PhaseOPD. In addition, PhaseOPD uses generation dynamics and the marginal utility of task-specific supervision to detect diminishing returns. It terminates the remaining rollout once no further teacher query is needed, thereby reducing computational overhead. This constitutes the second level of adaptivity in PhaseOPD and follows Occam’s razor: introduce supervision only when necessary. In summary, our main contributions are threefold: (1) We revisit teacher organization in multi-teacher on-policy distillation by introducing a generation-dynamics dimension orthogonal to the task dimension. We further identify the mismatch between teacher supervision and denoising dynamics, a problem that task-level OPD cannot adequately characterize. (2) We propose PhaseOPD, which uses the student’s dynamics to identify, for each task-specific teacher, the generation intervals where its supervision is most valuable and schedules queries accordingly. This reduces cross-stage interference and unnecessary over-constraint. (3) We introduce a dynamic truncation strategy that immediately terminates the subsequent rollout once the supervision signals determine the required teacher-query positions, avoiding redundant computation.

sections.heading: 2 Motivation
sections.text: Mainstream OPD paradigms overlook that different specialized teacher capabilities should align with the characteristics of different denoising stages. This oversight can create temporal conflicts between teacher supervision and denoising dynamics. If a teacher specializing in local details intervenes before the global structure stabilizes, its supervision may prematurely steer the model toward local optimization objectives and disrupt primary structure formation. Meanwhile, because local details rely on an established global structure as their underlying carrier, the absence of a stable structural foundation also prevents detail-oriented supervision from fully realizing its value . Conversely, once the primary structure has converged and the model has entered the local refinement stage, continued strong structural supervision may unnecessarily constrain subsequent detail enhancement. More generally, even if a teacher’s objective is reasonable, applying its supervision at an incompatible generation stage may still produce low-value or even competing gradients. This issue resembles course scheduling in education. A student’s learning outcome depends not only on what is taught, but also on whether the course sequence matches the student’s current developmental stage. The visualization in Fig. 1 further shows how teacher-query and supervision-skipping timing affect overall performance. Teachers specializing in semantic structure achieve the best results when queried early in the generation stage. In contrast, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) teachers focusing on textual content and teachers specializing in aesthetic quality yield greater supervisory benefits during the middle and late stages, respectively.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: This section presents PhaseOPD’s overall framework, extending task-level teacher organization to generation-dynamics-aware teacher coordination. We first introduce an adaptive generation-stage identification module that analyzes the student model’s own generation trajectory to determine the generative responsibility of its current state. Based on the identified stage, PhaseOPD employs a dynamic teacher-routing mechanism that assigns teachers with different capabilities to the generation stages where their supervision is most effective, thereby reducing cross-stage supervision conflicts. Finally, we propose a dynamic rollout truncation mechanism to eliminate redundant computation. Figure 2 : Overall framework of our method

sections.heading: 3.2 Online Generative Phase Perception
sections.text: Existing OPD methods select teachers primarily according to task categories. However, a teacher’s supervisory value varies across states and generation stages. To allocate teacher supervision on demand following the inherent generation dynamics, PhaseOPD detects stage transitions during the student model’s on-policy rollout and adaptively determines when each teacher should provide supervision.

sections.heading: 3.3 Teacher-Conditioned Phase Routing
sections.text: Building on the three generation stages identified in Sec. 3.2 , we establish a correspondence between generation stages and supervision objectives, enabling each specialized teacher to contribute during the stage in which its supervision is most valuable. Stage I: Global Structure Formation . Since the overall structure has not yet fully formed at this stage, local details lack a stable structural foundation. This stage is therefore better suited to supervision targeting global structural consistency, such as GenEval. We set the teacher query position to the sampling position immediately preceding the left boundary, namely k L − 1 k_{\mathrm{L}}-1 . This choice is motivated by the observation that states too close to the pure-noise endpoint lack well-defined structure. Selecting the last sampling position before the left boundary thus allows structure-related supervision to be applied once structural information has begun to emerge, but before local details become dominant. Stage II: Local Content Generation . In Stage II, the primary structure provides a relatively stable spatial foundation for local content, while local semantics and details continue to emerge and evolve. This stage is therefore well suited to specialized teachers that focus on local content accuracy, such as OCR teachers. We randomly sample a supervision point within Stage II to cover varying degrees of local content formation, avoid excessive reliance on a single generation position, and improve the adaptability of local content supervision to variations in states within this stage. Stage III: Visual Aesthetic Enhancement . In the final stage of generation, the image approaches convergence, with the primary structure and local details remaining largely unchanged. This stability provides a foundation for aesthetic optimization, making this stage well suited to specialized aesthetic teachers, such as Aesthetic. In Stage III, we set the teacher query position to the first sampling position after the right boundary, namely k R + 1 k_{\mathrm{R}}+1 . This choice lets aesthetic supervision act on a state where the primary structure and local content are already stable, while still leaving room for further refinement. Once the supervision position for the current sample is determined, the teacher provides supervision only at the corresponding student-visited state, preserving the basic formulation of on-policy distillation while reducing cross-stage supervision mismatch and redundant trajectory computation. sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: This chapter evaluates PhaseOPD around three questions: (1) whether staged querying can improve both generation quality and training cost with the primary teacher group; (2) whether these gains generalize across teacher combinations, student backbones, and task types; and (3) what roles adaptive triggering and early termination play, and why online signals can identify effective querying stages. We present the main results, generalization experiments, component ablations, and mechanistic analyses in that order. Detailed settings and additional results are provided in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Implementation Details & Training Data
sections.text: We initialize an SD3.5-Medium student from the base model and train rank-32 LoRA adapters at 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution using frozen Aesthetic, GenEval, and OCR teachers. Our default configuration uses 16-step on-policy rollouts, equal task sampling, 3,000 updates, and four H20 GPUs. Full data construction, guidance scales, and optimization settings are provided in Appendix B.1 .

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: We use AES on DrawBench, GenEval, and OCR as the primary metrics for aesthetics, compositional alignment, and text rendering. We additionally report HPSv3, PickScore, and SigLIP where applicable, and use ImageReward and VQAScore as held-out diagnostics.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare against the SD3.5-M base model, three single-teacher models, DanceOPD, and DiffusionOPD. Our default model augments DanceOPD with phase-aware querying; we additionally apply the same mechanism to DiffusionOPD and FlowOPD and evaluate its transfer to the BAGEL and FLUX backbones.

sections.heading: 4.4 Generalization Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate the cross-backbone generalization of our method in two complementary settings. The BAGEL experiments change both the generative backbone and the task formulation, extending text-to-image generation to global and local editing. As shown in Fig. 7 , our method improves text-to-image generation and local editing, remains competitive on global editing, and reduces overall training cost. The FLUX experiments retain the multi-teacher text-to-image generation setting and replace only the underlying generative model. Tab. 3 shows that our method outperforms DanceOPD across all generation quality metrics while achieving higher training efficiency. Together, these experiments demonstrate that phase-aware querying is not tied to the specific generation process of SD3.5-M but can generalize across model architectures and task formulations, consistently improving the quality–cost trade-off.

sections.heading: 4.6 Mechanism Analysis
sections.text: Controlled single-teacher experiments on phase sensitivity are provided in Appendix B.4 . To analyze the querying preferences of different teachers during generation, we summarize the query positions selected by our method under three OPD training objectives in Fig. 8 . GenEval queries are concentrated primarily in the early stages, OCR queries favor the middle stages, and Aesthetic queries span both early and late stages. Although the precise peaks vary with the underlying training objective, the overall phase preferences of the three teachers remain consistent. These results indicate that different teachers supervise at different generation stages, while our method adapts query positions to the student’s actual trajectory rather than relying on fixed timesteps.

sections.heading: Student dynamics recover this ordering online
sections.text: Fig. 9 shows the two online signals used by the adaptive trigger: the change in the spatial-scale revision ratio, Δ ​ F k = F k − F k − 1 \Delta F_{k}=F_{k}-F_{k-1} , and its first-order difference, g k = Δ ​ F k − Δ ​ F k − 1 g_{k}=\Delta F_{k}-\Delta F_{k-1} . As the rollout progresses, Δ ​ F k \Delta F_{k} rises rapidly in the early stages and reaches a peak, then declines substantially before settling into small, stable fluctuations in the later stages. The detector identifies stage boundaries when g k g_{k} approaches zero after sustained increases and decreases in Δ ​ F k \Delta F_{k} , respectively, following the criterion in Sec. 3.2 . These transitions separate the early rise, intermediate decline, and later stabilization of the spatial-scale revision signal. Because both signals are computed solely from current and past student states, phase boundaries can be identified causally online without access to future rollout states.

sections.heading: 4.7 User Preference Study
sections.text: To evaluate the generated results from a human perceptual perspective, we conduct a double-blind user preference study comparing our method against DanceOPD and DiffusionOPD in pairwise comparisons. Each pair of candidate images is generated using the same text prompt, random seed, and inference configuration and presented in a randomized order. Participants are unaware of which method produced each image and are asked to select the better result based on overall visual quality, text alignment, and content completeness, or to indicate a tie. As shown in Fig. 10 , our method receives higher user preference rates against both multi-teacher distillation baselines. These findings are consistent with the automatic evaluations, indicating that the improvements from phase-aware querying translate into perceptible gains in generation quality rather than merely numerical improvements on specific evaluation metrics.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented PhaseOPD, which connects teacher supervision timing with early termination of student rollouts. Causal signals from predicted-clean latent revisions identify teacher-specific query states, allowing single-query distillation to proceed without generating the remaining trajectory. Experiments show fewer rollout steps, lower training cost, the strongest GenEval score in our comparison, and faster first-hour gains on GenEval and OCR. The results support jointly designing where to learn and how far to roll out as a practical route to efficient multi-capability post-training.

sections.heading: A.1 Post-training generative models.
sections.text: Diffusion models [ 6 ] and flow matching [ 10 ] learn iterative transformations between noise and data; rectified-flow transformers scale this approach to high-resolution text-to-image synthesis [ 4 ] . Post-training methods align these models with downstream objectives. DDPO treats denoising as a sequential decision process and applies policy gradients to image rewards [ 3 ] ; Diffusion-DPO instead learns from pairwise preferences [ 15 ] . Flow-GRPO extends online policy optimization to flow matching and reduces the number of training denoising steps [ 11 ] . PhaseOPD integrates expert capabilities and reduces rollout computation by identifying supervision states online.

sections.heading: A.2 On-policy capability transfer.
sections.text: Training on student-generated sequences is a central principle of on-policy language-model distillation [ 1 ] . DiffusionOPD transfers task-specific teachers along student trajectories using a continuous-state distillation formulation [ 8 ] . Flow-OPD combines specialized teachers, task routing, and dense trajectory supervision for flow models [ 5 ] . DanceOPD routes each sample to one generative field and uses velocity regression at a low-noise student state [ 20 ] . We retain task-specific teachers and single-query regression. Our contribution concerns how student dynamics determine the query state and the minimum rollout prefix needed to select it; we do not claim a new regression loss or single-query distillation principle.

sections.heading: A.3 Stage specialization and efficient sampling.
sections.text: eDiff-I assigns separately trained denoisers to different synthesis stages [ 2 ] , demonstrating the usefulness of time-dependent specialization. PhaseOPD instead schedules supervision from capability-specific teachers using the evolving student state, producing one student for inference. Progressive distillation reduces the number of steps required to generate a completed sample [ 14 ] . Our early stopping serves a different purpose: it removes the unneeded suffix of a training trajectory once its supervision state is known. It leaves the inference procedure unchanged and can be studied independently of methods that accelerate completed-image sampling.

sections.heading: A.4 On-Policy Distillation
sections.text: On-policy distillation supervises students on self-generated states, reducing training–generation mismatch [ 1 ] . For visual generation, Flow-OPD combines task routing with dense trajectory supervision [ 5 ] , while DiffusionOPD derives a continuous-state distillation objective [ 8 ] . Flow3D-OPD extends multi-teacher transfer to 3D geometry [ 13 ] , and DanceOPD uses one low-noise velocity query per sample [ 20 ] . These methods leave a complementary timing question: which state best supports each teacher’s objective, and how much rollout is needed to select it? PhaseOPD uses student dynamics to determine teacher-specific query positions and skips the remaining rollout once all query decisions are finalized.

sections.heading: Implementation Details & Training Data.
sections.text: We use SD3.5-Medium as the base model for multi-teacher distillation at a resolution of 512 × 512 512\times 512 . The student is initialized from the base model and trained using LoRA with rank r = 32 r=32 and scaling factor α = 64 \alpha=64 . We use frozen task-specific teachers for Aesthetic, GenEval, and OCR, training the student to match their velocity predictions at selected generation states rather than directly optimizing reward scores. For Aesthetic, we use text prompts from Pick-a-Pic; for GenEval and OCR, we follow the training splits used in FlowGRPO. After deduplicating prompts, removing overlaps with the designated test splits, and setting aside fixed validation sets, we retain 25,106, 32,943, and 19,392 training prompts for the three tasks, respectively. Training uses 16-step online student rollouts, with a classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale of 4.5 for the student and 4.5, 1.0, and 4.5 for the three teachers, respectively. Tasks are sampled with equal probability, and all distillation loss weights are set to 1. The main experiments are run on four H20 GPUs for 3,000 updates with a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} .

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate image aesthetic quality using Aesthetic Score (AES) on DrawBench and assess semantic alignment and text-generation accuracy using GenEval and OCR, respectively. We additionally report HPSv3, PickScore, SigLIP, ImageReward, and VQAScore as auxiliary evaluation metrics.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare the base model, three single-teacher models, and representative multi-teacher online policy distillation methods, including DanceOPD and DiffusionOPD. The base and single-teacher models serve as references for individual capabilities, while the multi-teacher methods evaluate different knowledge-fusion strategies. By default, we use DanceOPD as the underlying distillation objective and refer to its variant augmented with phase-aware querying as Ours . When the same strategy is applied to other objectives, we use the names “DiffusionOPD + Ours” and “FlowOPD + Ours.” In addition to the main experiments on SD3.5-M, we compare DanceOPD with Ours on the BAGEL and FLUX backbones to separate the effects of teacher combinations, generative backbones, and task types.

sections.heading: B.2 Time to Matched Quality
sections.text: To examine whether the training-time advantage persists at comparable quality, we measure the wall-clock time required to reach a common threshold for each task. Fig. 11 reports results for Aesthetic ≥ 5.70 \geq 5.70 , GenEval ≥ 0.89 \geq 0.89 , and OCR ≥ 0.90 \geq 0.90 . Ours reaches these targets in 16.19, 32.38, and 16.19 minutes, respectively, earlier than both DanceOPD and DiffusionOPD. These gains complement the final-checkpoint comparisons, showing that phase-aware querying and early skipping speed up capability acquisition across all three objectives. sections.heading: B.3 Independent Diagnostic Evaluation
sections.text: We use independent diagnostic metrics to assess whether improvements extend beyond the rewards used to train the teachers. The seven models in each comparison are evaluated on GenAI-Bench-1600 with shared prompts, seeds, and inference settings: 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution, 40 sampling steps, and CFG 4.5. ImageReward uses ImageReward-v1.0, while VQAScore uses CLIP-FlanT5-XXL through t2v-metrics==3.0 . The results in Tabs. 1 and 2 show that Ours improves both diagnostic metrics over the multi-teacher baselines under both teacher combinations. This consistency supports transfer beyond the teacher-specific training objectives.

sections.heading: Phase Sensitivity of Teacher Supervision.
sections.text: Different teacher models exhibit different sensitivities to the querying phase. We conduct separate training runs with the Aesthetic, GenEval, and OCR teachers, restricting queries to R1 (steps 1–4), R2 (5–8), R3 (9–12), or R4 (13–16). Across these experiments, only the teacher query interval is varied. Fig. 12 reports changes in the corresponding target metric relative to the Beta querying strategy, reflecting each teacher’s individual phase preference rather than the joint performance of a multi-teacher model. Figure 12 : Stage sensitivity of teacher supervision. The three panels report Aesthetic, GenEval, and OCR gains from controlled single-teacher experiments. Each bar shows the change relative to the Beta query strategy when queries are restricted to the corresponding generation interval. The GenEval teacher exhibits a clear preference for early-stage supervision, with its largest relative gain occurring in R1. Effective supervision from the OCR teacher concentrates in the middle stages, with the largest relative gain in R2 and the second-largest in R3. The Aesthetic teacher achieves its highest relative gain in R3, followed by R2. R4 underperforms the Beta strategy for all three teachers, indicating that states closer to the trajectory endpoint do not consistently provide more effective teacher supervision. These distinct temporal response profiles provide controlled experimental evidence for determining query timing based on the teacher type and the student’s current state.

Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) enables flow-matching models to acquire complementary capabilities from specialized teachers through supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, different evaluation dimensions (e.g., aesthetics and OCR accuracy) and tasks (e.g., image generation and editing) emphasize different aspects of the denoising process, suggesting that their effective supervision may occur at different stages. Existing methods typically select supervision states from predefined timestep distributions, which may overlook these phase-dependent differences with unnecessary computation overhead. This motivates two critical timing decisions: when to adaptively query teachers for effective supervision based on the evolving generative process, and when to skip the remaining rollout to avoid redundant computation, i.e. , timing matters twice . In this paper, we introduce PhaseOPD , a phase-aware query-and-skip framework that identifies generative phases online from revisions of predicted-clean latents, using existing student velocity predictions without additional model evaluations. For each task-assigned teacher, PhaseOPD selects a supervision state based on its phase preference and skips the unused rollout suffix once all query decisions are finalized, preserving the single-query velocity-distillation objective. On SD3.5-M, PhaseOPD executes only 5.56 of 16 rollout positions per local batch (65.2% fewer), reducing training time by 41.3% relative to DanceOPD while improving Aesthetic, GenEval, and OCR scores. 1 Introduction Figure 1 : Teacher supervision is not equally useful throughout denoising: semantic composition, text rendering, and aesthetics benefit most from different query intervals. This motivates adapting query timing to each teacher-task pair and terminating the rollout after the required queries, rather than using a shared preset schedule and completing every denoising step. In recent years, diffusion and flow-matching models have made significant progress in image generation [ 7 , 9 , 12 , 16 , 18 ] . The research focus has gradually shifted from improving basic generative capabilities to aligning models with challenging task-specific objectives and preferences through post-training. In complex applications, generative models must satisfy multiple criteria simultaneously, including accurate semantic composition, coherent spatial structure, high-quality local details, and visual appearance aligned with human preferences. Improving multiple visual objectives within a unified model has therefore become an important challenge in generative model post-training. Previous studies have mainly combined reward signals from different evaluation dimensions using weighted aggregation and optimized the generation distribution of pretrained models through reinforcement learning [ 19 , 17 ] . However, such methods not only rely on sparse scalar rewards for optimization, but also suffer from competing update directions induced by heterogeneous rewards, often resulting in gradient interference and imbalanced capabilities. To mitigate reward sparsity and gradient conflicts in joint multi-objective optimization, recent studies have introduced On-Policy Distillation (OPD) into generative models [ 5 , 8 , 20 ] . Instead of directly optimizing a single policy with multiple rewards, multi-teacher OPD first trains specialized teachers independently for different objectives. These teachers then provide supervision on the student’s own generation trajectories, integrating diverse generative capabilities into a unified student model. Although OPD provides an effective approach to multi-objective optimization, existing OPD paradigms do not adequately characterize how the value of each task-specific teacher’s supervision changes across generation stages. Because each teacher is trained for a distinct objective, the key question is which part of the student’s trajectory provides the most effective supervision for that teacher and its corresponding task—not which teacher should be assigned to a given stage. This raises two connected questions: for each teacher-task pair, at what stage should the student be queried to obtain the most useful supervision? Once the relevant query for each task has been completed, when can the remaining rollout be terminated to avoid redundant computation? When query timing is not specified for each teacher-task pair, it remains unclear whether a chosen supervision stage is well suited to that teacher’s objective. This matters because denoising follows a stage-dependent pattern: early stages focus on constructing global semantics, intermediate stages gradually shift toward local content generation, and later stages place greater emphasis on refining details and visual aesthetics. These evolving responsibilities mean that the utility of a given teacher’s guidance depends on whether the student’s state at a particular stage is suitable for that teacher’s corresponding objective. Thus, supervision timing should be determined for each teacher-task pair, rather than by assigning teachers to stages in isolation. Beyond effectively scheduling teacher supervision, avoiding unnecessary computational overhead is another important challenge for multi-teacher OPD. Obtaining teacher supervision requires long and continuous rollouts of student trajectories, which introduces considerable computational costs. More importantly, once all necessary teacher queries have been completed, or once the denoising process is close to convergence and the latent representation has become nearly stationary, continuing the remaining rollout provides little additional information for distillation. It may even introduce optimization conflicts due to a mismatch between teacher supervision and generation dynamics. Therefore, skipping redundant trajectory supervision while preserving its effectiveness is crucial to improving OPD training efficiency. Appendix. A discusses related work in detail. Building on these insights, we propose PhaseOPD, a dual timing-adaptive policy distillation framework that uses the student’s generation dynamics to schedule each task-specific teacher at the stages where its supervision is most useful. Unlike existing methods that focus primarily on task-level teacher selection without jointly optimizing teacher-query timing and trajectory length, PhaseOPD identifies a suitable query interval for each teacher-task pair from the student’s evolving trajectory. For example, it schedules structure-oriented supervision during global layout and primary structure formation, supervision for objectives involving both structure and detail during the transition toward semantic content and salient details, and visual-quality supervision during later texture and appearance refinement. The task-specific teacher defines what is supervised, while the trajectory dynamics determine when its supervision is applied. This constitutes the first level of adaptivity in PhaseOPD. In addition, PhaseOPD uses generation dynamics and the marginal utility of task-specific supervision to detect diminishing returns. It terminates the remaining rollout once no further teacher query is needed, thereby reducing computational overhead. This constitutes the second level of adaptivity in PhaseOPD and follows Occam’s razor: introduce supervision only when necessary. In summary, our main contributions are threefold: (1) We revisit teacher organization in multi-teacher on-policy distillation by introducing a generation-dynamics dimension orthogonal to the task dimension. We further identify the mismatch between teacher supervision and denoising dynamics, a problem that task-level OPD cannot adequately characterize. (2) We propose PhaseOPD, which uses the student’s dynamics to identify, for each task-specific teacher, the generation intervals where its supervision is most valuable and schedules queries accordingly. This reduces cross-stage interference and unnecessary over-constraint. (3) We introduce a dynamic truncation strategy that immediately terminates the subsequent rollout once the supervision signals determine the required teacher-query positions, avoiding redundant computation. 2 Motivation Mainstream OPD paradigms overlook that different specialized teacher capabilities should align with the characteristics of different denoising stages. This oversight can create temporal conflicts between teacher supervision and denoising dynamics. If a teacher specializing in local details intervenes before the global structure stabilizes, its supervision may prematurely steer the model toward local optimization objectives and disrupt primary structure formation. Meanwhile, because local details rely on an established global structure as their underlying carrier, the absence of a stable structural foundation also prevents detail-oriented supervision from fully realizing its value . Conversely, once the primary structure has converged and the model has entered the local refinement stage, continued strong structural supervision may unnecessarily constrain subsequent detail enhancement. More generally, even if a teacher’s objective is reasonable, applying its supervision at an incompatible generation stage may still produce low-value or even competing gradients. This issue resembles course scheduling in education. A student’s learning outcome depends not only on what is taught, but also on whether the course sequence matches the student’s current developmental stage. The visualization in Fig. 1 further shows how teacher-query and supervision-skipping timing affect overall performance. Teachers specializing in semantic structure achieve the best results when queried early in the generation stage. In contrast, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) teachers focusing on textual content and teachers specializing in aesthetic quality yield greater supervisory benefits during the middle and late stages, respectively. 3 Method This section presents PhaseOPD’s overall framework, extending task-level teacher organization to generation-dynamics-aware teacher coordination. We first introduce an adaptive generation-stage identification module that analyzes the student model’s own generation trajectory to determine the generative responsibility of its current state. Based on the identified stage, PhaseOPD employs a dynamic teacher-routing mechanism that assigns teachers with different capabilities to the generation stages where their supervision is most effective, thereby reducing cross-stage supervision conflicts. Finally, we propose a dynamic rollout truncation mechanism to eliminate redundant computation. We set the teacher query position to the sampling position immediately preceding the left boundary, namely k L − 1 k_{\mathrm{L}}-1 . This choice is motivated by the observation that states too close to the pure-noise endpoint lack well-defined structure. Selecting the last sampling position before the left boundary thus allows structure-related supervision to be applied once structural information has begun to emerge, but before local details become dominant. Stage II: Local Content Generation . In Stage II, the primary structure provides a relatively stable spatial foundation for local content, while local semantics and details continue to emerge and evolve. This stage is therefore well suited to specialized teachers that focus on local content accuracy, such as OCR teachers. Causal signals from predicted-clean latent revisions identify teacher-specific query states, allowing single-query distillation to proceed without generating the remaining trajectory.
